claims.text: Aggressive service conditions such as high strain rate or low temperature trigger a reduction in chemical randomness in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The reduction in chemical randomness promotes nanoscale short-range ordering within the alloy matrix.
Nanoscale ordered clusters hinder dislocation motion.
The impediment of dislocation motion by short-range-ordered clusters reduces toughness.
The proposed short-range-ordered clusters are distributed within the matrix rather than occurring as conventional grain-boundary precipitates.
The short-range-ordered clusters may align along specific crystallographic planes.
Sluggish diffusion and large lattice distortion may lower the local energy barrier for atomic rearrangement under aggressive loading or low-temperature conditions.
Brittleness can emerge while long-range intermetallic phases and grain-boundary segregation remain suppressed.
Compared with the moderate-condition baseline, aggressive-condition samples will exhibit increased nanoscale short-range order.
The increase in nanoscale short-range order will be accompanied by reduced fracture toughness.
Embrittlement under aggressive conditions will occur without conventional grain-boundary precipitation.
The moderate-condition, as-homogenized baseline retains a fully disordered structure and high toughness.
High strain rate or cryogenic temperature can provide sufficient driving force for local atomic rearrangements that produce short-range order.
At elevated temperature or low mechanical drive, atomic mobility remains too sluggish to promote short-range order and the alloy maintains high toughness.

contradictions.description: Low or cryogenic temperature is said to enable atomic rearrangement and SRO, whereas elevated temperature is said to leave atomic mobility too sluggish for SRO. This temperature dependence is internally counterintuitive and is not reconciled by a stated non-diffusive or stress-assisted ordering pathway.
